title: If you are able
hookLine: Hajj is due once in a lifetime on those with health, means and safety (3:97)

cards: Three times a man asks the same question, and twice the answer is silence. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ has just told the people that Allah has made the pilgrimage a duty for them.
The man calls out: every year, Messenger of Allah? The Prophet says nothing. The man asks again.
Silence. He asks a third time. And the answer, kept in Sahih Muslim, isn't the one he expected: if I said yes, it would become a duty, and you would not be able to do it.

teach.h: FOR HIM WHO CAN FIND A WAY.
teach.b: First, the verse. Surah three of the Qur'an, in Pickthall's words: "And pilgrimage to the House is a duty unto Allah for mankind, for him who can find a way thither."
The House is the Kaaba in Mecca, and the duty comes with its condition already attached: for the one who can find a way. Second, the word.
Istita'ah means being able, having the capacity; it's the word jurists use for that condition. The duty of Hajj isn't on everyone in general. It's on the one who is able.

Scholars of the schools spell it out and differ on some details, but the broad shape is health enough to make the journey, the means to pay for it without leaving one's family short, and a road safe enough to travel.
A person missing one of those isn't failing a duty; for them, it isn't yet due. Fourth, how often. That's where the man's question comes in.
Some readers hear the Prophet's silence as a mercy: he doesn't add to what's been asked.
And the report goes on: he tells the people to leave him be as long as he leaves them be, and to do what they're commanded as far as they're able.
Scholars read it this way: the duty is once in a lifetime, for those who can, and anything more is voluntary. So the condition is part of the pillar itself. For some, the way opens early.
For some, it takes a lifetime of saving. For some, it never becomes possible, and they keep the intention.

how: Muslims who have the health, money and safe passage go on Hajj once in their lives; some save for years, and those who cannot go keep the intention and sometimes, by their school's rules, send someone in their place.

o: a blessing from an imam before setting out for Mecca
being able: health, means and a safe road to make Hajj
the yearly duty to visit Mecca for every Muslim

s: every Muslim must go on Hajj, whatever their health or money
the verse sets the condition itself: for him who can find a way.
Hajj is due once in a lifetime
the Prophet would not make it yearly: if he had said yes, people would not have been able.
a person who can't afford Hajj is failing a duty
for someone without the means, it isn't yet due.

games.q: you're the Prophet. a man asks, three times, whether Hajj is due every year. what do you answer?
o: if I said yes, it would become a duty, and you would not be able.
only in the years you feel ready.
games.why: he answers that saying yes would make it a duty no one could keep. once in a lifetime, for those who are able.

practice: If you're Muslim and you pray, ask in your own words for the means and the health to make the journey one day, or give thanks if you already have.
If not, think of one journey you've long wanted to make, one that matters to you, and notice what stands between you and it: health, money, time, safety. No need to solve it; just see it clearly.

wordCard.voice: Istita'ah. Being able: the condition the Qur'an sets on Hajj, for the one who can find a way. Today's word.

orig.note: being able, capacity: the jurists' word for the condition on Hajj.

carryVoice: Your line: once, if able. Hajj waits until a person can go. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: And pilgrimage to the House is a duty unto Allah for mankind, for him who can find a way thither.
